setupSteps: Set the hooks. FitPlate beginner choice: set the bar in the rack at about upper-chest height (est.), so you only need to dip slightly to get under it and do not have to stand on your toes to unrack. Sources differ: one guide says roughly eye level or slightly above, others say shoulder or upper-chest level. Pick the height where you unrack with a small bend of the knees and no lean.

Set the safeties. Place the pins or straps just below the lowest point of your press, about chest-to-upper-chest height (est.; no press-specific standard found, sources say "just below shoulder level"). Test with the empty bar: lower it onto the safeties to confirm it clears you.

Choose the load. Start with the empty bar (about 20 kg for a standard Olympic bar, est.; check the bar label, lighter training bars exist). Beginner guides suggest empty-bar sets of 5-12 reps first; do not add weight until sets are clean.
Collars or clips on every loaded set. Fit them on both ends and load both sides evenly; a rep-fitness article calls collars mandatory for the overhead press because plates can shift.
Feet: about hip-to-shoulder width, toes slightly out, weight over the whole foot (mid-foot). Feet too close together makes balance harder.

Grip: overhand, hands just outside shoulder width (est.), so that at the bottom the forearms are close to vertical and the wrists are above the elbows. Sources agree on "just outside the shoulders"; wider shoulders often prefer a slightly wider grip.
Hold the bar low in the palm with the thumbs wrapped, the wrist straight (bar over the wrist and forearm, not resting back on bent fingers).
Elbows slightly in front of the bar (not flared out to the sides), pointing forward and slightly down; this is the front-rack position.
Get under the bar with the bar resting on the front of the shoulders and upper chest; stand up to lift it off the hooks.
Step back one or two small steps and set your feet. Check that you are clear of the hooks and other people.
Brace: squeeze the glutes, pull the ribs down, tighten the abdominals as if bracing for a light punch; knees locked but not hyper-extended (soft-straight).

Seated version (regression): use an upright bench with a back pad (about 75-90 degrees, sources vary; est.), feet flat, lower back against the pad with a natural curve only (not a hard arch), bar at upper-chest height on the rack or taken from a spotter or staff the first time.
Spotter or staff: not essential with correct safeties, but ask staff to watch the first session and check the pin height.

steps.title: Take the bar out of the rack
steps.action: Dip under the bar, bar on the front shoulders, lift it off the hooks by standing up.
steps.feel: Weight on the front of the shoulders and legs.
steps.visualCheck: Front: elbows just in front of the bar, wrists straight. Side: the bar over mid-foot.

steps.title: Step back and set your feet
steps.action: Take one or two small steps back, feet hip to shoulder width.
steps.visualCheck: Front: feet even. Side: knees soft-straight.

steps.title: Brace the glutes and abdominals
steps.action: Squeeze the glutes, ribs down, belly tight.
steps.breathing: Breathe in and brace, do not hold for long.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ribs not flared; lower back not arched.

steps.title: Start the press
steps.action: Press the bar up from the shoulders; the elbows stay slightly in front.
steps.breathing: Start breathing out as the bar moves.
steps.visualCheck: Front: forearms near vertical; bar does not drift forward.

steps.title: Move the head back as the bar passes the face
steps.action: Tip the head back slightly (move the whole head, not just the chin) so the bar travels close to the face in a straight line.
steps.feel: Bar skims past the nose and forehead.
steps.visualCheck: Side: bar moves up in a near-vertical line; the torso does not lean back.

steps.title: Push the head through as the bar clears the forehead
steps.action: Once the bar is above the forehead, push the head and chest forward through the arms so the bar finishes over the body.
steps.feel: Shoulders and triceps drive the last part.
steps.visualCheck: Front: the bar moving to centre; side: head slightly forward of the bar.

steps.title: Lock out over mid-foot
steps.action: Straighten the elbows fully, shrug slightly to lock out with the bar over the middle of the feet (the Starting Strength school calls this the active shrug).
steps.feel: Arms straight, shoulders up near the ears, trunk tight.
steps.visualCheck: Front: both wrists over the shoulders, bar level. Side: bar, shoulder, hip and ankle roughly in one vertical line.

steps.title: Pause briefly
steps.visualCheck: Front: no sway; side: no lean-back.

steps.title: Lower under control
steps.action: Lower the bar back to the front shoulders along the same line; move the head back as it passes the face and then forward again.
steps.feel: Shoulders and triceps control the lowering.
steps.visualCheck: Side: straight path, trunk still; front: elbows end slightly in front of the bar.

steps.title: Rerack after the last rep
steps.action: After the final rep, walk forward until the bar touches the hooks, check both sides, then lower the bar onto them gently.
steps.visualCheck: Front: both ends of the bar sit in the hooks; never rerack by feel or in a hurry (a missed hook can drop the bar on you, Starting Strength).

commonMistakes.title: Leaning back and arching the lower back
commonMistakes.text: Leaning back and arching the lower back. Why: the lumbar spine bends backward to put the bar overhead, which loads the lower-back joints and discs, and a physiotherapy-oriented source calls it the most common cause of low back pain from the press (coach-level). Fix: squeeze the glutes, ribs down, lighter bar, or use a seated press with back support or a machine (Gym 33).

commonMistakes.title: Pushing the bar out in front of the face
commonMistakes.text: Pushing the bar out in front of the face. Why: a forward bar path makes the lift harder and pulls you off balance. Fix: move the head back so the bar goes straight up, then push the head through.

commonMistakes.title: Elbows flared to the sides
commonMistakes.text: Elbows flared to the sides. Why: shortens the path and stresses the shoulder front. Fix: keep the elbows slightly in front of the bar and the forearms near vertical.

commonMistakes.title: Not locking out over mid-foot
commonMistakes.text: Not locking out over mid-foot. Why: the bar over the toes or heels means balance is poor and the shoulders can tire early. Fix: finish with the bar over the middle of the foot, head through, a small shrug.

commonMistakes.title: Using the legs (accidental push press)
commonMistakes.text: Using the legs (accidental push press). Why: a knee dip makes it a different lift and hides weak shoulders. Fix: knees straight, a slow strict press, drop the load.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath for long
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath for long. Why: raises blood pressure briefly. Fix: brace, press, breathe out near the top; do not hold through the whole set.

commonMistakes.title: No collars or uneven plates
commonMistakes.text: No collars or uneven plates. Why: a plate can slide and tip the bar overhead. Fix: collars every loaded set and a tug test.

commonMistakes.title: Safeties too low, too high or not set
commonMistakes.text: Safeties too low, too high or not set. Why: pins too low do not catch a missed rep; too high get in the way. Fix: set just below the lowest bar position and test with an empty bar (no press-specific standard found).

commonMistakes.title: Reracking by feel
commonMistakes.text: Reracking by feel. Why: a missed hook can drop the bar on you. Fix: walk forward until the bar touches the uprights, look, and lower slowly.

commonMistakes.title: Going too heavy too soon
commonMistakes.text: Going too heavy too soon. Why: form breaks, spine and shoulder risk. Fix: empty bar first, add 1.25-2.5 kg when all sets are clean.

safetyNotes: Safeties and collars: set the pins just below the lowest bar position, use collars on every loaded set, rerack only after the bar touches the uprights.

Shoulder impingement: the evidence is mixed. A 2012 meta-analysis (Timmons) found less upward rotation of the shoulder blade in people with impingement, while a 2016 meta-analysis (Park) found no difference in subacromial space; no study was found that shows the barbell press causes impingement. Practical advice: press in the scapular plane (elbows slightly in front), avoid shrugging high early, avoid behind-the-neck, stop with sharp or pinching pain.

Lower back: keep ribs down and glutes tight; stop if you feel a pinch or pain in the lower back. Strength coaches and Barbell Medicine suggest limiting end-range back extension and using a seated back-supported press or a staggered stance during early spondylolysis; this is coach-level, and symptom-free spondylolysis is not an automatic ban.
High blood pressure: brace but do not hold the breath through the set; stop short of failure.
Spotter: not required if the safeties are correct, but ask staff to check your first session.
Gym etiquette: do not rack or unrack on only one side; strip plates after use; do not block the rack for long rests; wipe the bar; do not film other members.
